e23m-1.L: Art. VI, Sec. 16(3) lets the House expel a Member for disorderly behavior by a two-thirds vote of all its Members and caps suspension at 60 days. No conviction is needed (Osmeña v. Pendatun), but due process still applies.
e23m-1.A: First, his absence was already punished by two 60-day suspensions; expelling him for it punishes him twice and evades the cap. Second, the terrorist designation is the Anti-Terrorism Council’s act, not his conduct as a Member. Third, the dance video and asylum bid are private acts that disrupted no House proceeding. Finally, expelling him for killings never tried, without a hearing, denies due process.

e23m-2.C: Sec. 2 deprives theater owners of property without due process.
e23m-2.L: Police power requires a lawful subject and reasonable means; an ordinance must not be unreasonable (White Light). Compelling the free use of property for public purposes is a taking that requires just compensation (PPI v. COMELEC; Quezon City v. Ericta).
e23m-2.A: Informing the public is lawful, but the means fail. Screen time is what theaters sell; demanding it free appropriates rather than regulates it. TELEBAP differs: broadcasters use public airwaves under a franchise the State may condition. Cinemas hold only a business permit, which cannot be used to extract property.
e23m-2.R: Sec. 2 is void unless the city pays for the screen time.
